2f4ebff472d58347: The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. "The vulnerability exists within internal components of Remote Support," BeyondTrust said in a Thursday alert. "The components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages it received. Under the right conditions, this could be used to perform file operations on the appliance." Patches for the flaw have been pushed to all Remote Support SaaS customers as of October 9, 2026. Self-hosted customers of Remote Support running versions from 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 are advised to manually update to BT26-05-RS patch. Customers running a version older than 24.3.1 will be required to upgrade to a newer version to apply the fix. According to a timeline of events shared by BeyondTrust, Armory Castle is said to have exploited the flaw as a zero-day on a single self-hosted Remote Support appliance on August 29, 2026. Then, on September 27, 2026, "successful exploitation of another security device provider [became] public," it added, prompting it to initiate an investigation to hunt for similar activity. Armory Castle has a history of exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966) and Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, and CVE-2025-0282) appliances to break a wide range of sectors, including legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology, and governments, for long-term intelligence collection. It's known to be active since October 2023. "The actor uses a zero-day selectively against chosen targets, and once the vulnerability is public, the actor typically moves to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched," BeyondTrust said. "Our working assessment is that this actor selects high-value software targets in advance and keeps a working model of the products the actor targets in an AI context that it uses on an ongoing basis to develop exploit chains." Google-owned Mandiant, which shared additional details related to the exploitation activity, said a successful compromise is followed by the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and bidirectional encrypted command-and-control (C2) communication. The operator makes use of commercial VPN exit nodes and compromised home and small-office routers to blend into regular traffic, and then leverages the web shell as a conduit to escalate privileges, obtain full administrative control of the appliance, and establish persistence in a manner that survives reboots. The intrusion is characterized by efforts to facilitate credential theft by reading the appliance's stored secrets and abusing the administrative access to reach downstream systems and enable lateral movement. Details of the post-exploitation actions undertaken by the threat actor are listed below - - Gaining root-level control of the appliance host by copying the system shell executable (/bin/sh) to the file "/usr/bin/dbus-authd" and modifying its ownership to root and enabling Set User ID (SUID) permissions, causing it to be executed with the privileges of the file's owner. - Attempting to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database by using the proprietary "/ns/sbin/bt-secrets" Command Line Interface (CLI) utility to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. - Targeting the BeyondTrust configuration templates to obtain passwordless root privileges to the site service account and - Pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised administrator credentials and then launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. - Abusing the elevated administrative privileges to establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints and obtain full file-system access to those systems with an aim to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents for network reconnaissance. - Tunneling traffic through the BeyondTrust device via BARECLAW, a C-based custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler that relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. - Modifying "/ns/config/haproxy.conf" file to ensure BARECLAW is accessible directly from the internet. - Hindering detection efforts by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. "Throughout the intrusion, Armory Castle leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant researchers Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, and John Wolfram said. "Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed." Update The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), on October 16, 2026, released an advisory, urging organizations with affected BeyondTrust Remote Support to immediately take the following actions - - Apply the BT26-05-RS patch. - Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed. - Conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of potential compromise. - Isolate any suspected or confirmed compromised appliances, hunt for indicators of threat actor activity, including unrecognized privileged or administrative sessions, and collect a snapshot of virtual appliances or a forensic image for physical appliances. - Rebuild from a known-good state and apply the BT26-05-RS patch. The agency has also added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by October 19, 2026.
166fdf646185c6ed: BeyondTrust warned customers on Thursday to patch a critical flaw in its Remote Support (RS) that has been exploited in zero-day attacks since late August. Remote Support is the company's enterprise-grade support solution that helps IT service desks, help desks, and customer support teams troubleshoot issues remotely. Tracked as CVE-2026-102764, this actively exploited authentication bypass vulnerability lets unprivileged remote attackers perform file operations on unpatched appliances and affects RS 26.2.3 or earlier. BeyondTrust patched the security issue for all Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access SaaS customers on October 8, but self-hosted installations must be patched manually if automatic updates are not enabled. "While our internal testing has not identified any way for an attacker to exploit this vulnerability in Privileged Remote Access, PRA shares the affected code, so out of an abundance of caution, we have released the patch for PRA and recommend self-hosted Privileged Remote Access customers apply it immediately," BeyondTrust said. Although the company shared very limited details about the vulnerability, it said the zero-day was abused in the wild by a suspected China-nexus espionage actor tracked by Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) security researchers as "Armory Castle" (formerly UNC5221) and by cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike as "Warp Panda." According to Mandiant researchers, who spotted the initial attacks, Armory Castle hackers exploited the flaw to gain initial access and escalated to root privileges on compromised devices by enabling Set User ID (SUID) permissions. Next, they deployed new Sawfly web shell and Bareclaw tunneler malware, wiped logs to evade detection, and moved laterally through the victim's network using compromised Administrator credentials by opening remote sessions on downstream systems. "After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset," Mandiant said. "Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed." Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver tracks over 1,400 BeyondTrust remote support instances exposed online, but it provides no information on how many have already been secured or are honeypots. Armory Castle is known for targeting zero-day vulnerabilities in network edge appliances, including various Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966) and Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887, then CVE-2025-0282) appliances, since at least October 2023 to breach enterprise networks and drop new custom malware. Threat intelligence company Volexity also said in January 2024 that UNC5221 had backdoored more than 2,100 Ivanti appliances using the GiftedVisitor webshell in attacks chaining the CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887 zero-days. "In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed," Mandiant added. "It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764." CVE-2026-102764 is the latest in a string of BeyondTrust flaws that threat actors have exploited in the wild in recent years. Most recently, attackers exploited another critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-1731) affecting Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access appliances to establish WebSocket channels and deploy ransomware. The Chinese state-backed Silk Typhoon hacking group is also believed to have exploited two zero-days (CVE-2024-12356 and CVE-2024-12686) to breach BeyondTrust's systems and use a stolen API key to compromise 17 Remote Support SaaS instances, including the U.S. Treasury Department's instance. In the same campaign, Silk Typhoon has also targeted the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which administers U.S. sanctions programs, and the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), which reviews foreign investments for national security risks. BeyondTrust provides identity security services to over 20,000 customers worldwide, including government agencies and 75% of Fortune 100 companies. 92a3eccd55c658eb: BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs Ivanti, Cisco, and Palo Alto Networks all had vulnerabilities in edge devices come under fire this week. Now BeyondTrust joins the group. A week chock full of new high-severity and actively exploited edge vulnerabilities continues with a Chinese cyberattack built around a critical flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances. This week, Ivanti, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks all disclosed major, already abused vulnerabilities in their core edge technologies. Might as well throw one more on the pile, then. According to a BeyondTrust blog post, the China-nexus threat actor tracked by Mandiant as "Armory Castle" (formerly UNC5221, aka UTA0178) exploited a critical BeyondTrust Remote Support vulnerability as a zero-day starting on Aug. 29, 2026. The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, earned a 9.3 CVSS score and is derived from an internal messaging component that didn't properly validate the origin of incoming messages. It doesn't get much more serious than a critical bug in a remote access tool. IT teams use Remote Support to connect to and control computers and servers at a distance, and by exploiting it, attackers were able to do more or less the same. Dark Reading reached out to BeyondTrust for comment on this story. China vs. Edge Bugs: The Same Old Story Remote Support is a common enough enterprise IT solution. BeyondTrust claims to serve more than 20,000 customers, including 75 of the Fortune 100. Exactly how many of those customers use Remote Support specifically is unclear. The best estimate might have been made earlier this year, when an AI agent uncovered a 9.9 CVSS-rated pre-authentication flaw in Remote Support and its companion product, Privileged Remote Access (PRA). At the time, researchers found around 11,000 Remote Support instances exposed to the Internet, across the cloud and on-premises. This time around, attackers got to the bug before any blue team agents did. The exploitation was characterized by speed, in fact, as Armory Castle deployed its new custom PHP Webshell "SAWFLY" just 11 minutes after weaponizing the vulnerability. Then the cyber-espionage actor got to business. According to a a report from Mandiant and Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), Armory Castle shot straight for the appliance's built-in secrets management database, systematically searching for passwords, application programming interface (API) keys, and endpoint credentials, before dumping all admin credentials. c It established persistence with a script, combatted forensic analysts by deleting system, Web server, and application logs, and escalated from a standard service account to full admin privileges. That allowed it to launch remote sessions with downstream systems, perform internal network reconnaissance, and download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents from victims' desktops. It also debuted a second, new custom tool, "BARECLAW," for SOCKS5 tunnelling. It was able to do all that thanks to what Mandiant considered a "deep understanding" of BeyondTrust's technical innards. BeyondTrust made a CVE-2026-102764 patch available on Oct. 9 and implored organizations with on-prem Remote Support to update as soon as possible. All customers would be well advised to hunt for evidence of exploitation, and, wherever possible, severely restrict Internet exposure for their network management tools. Such advice is familiar — thought not always practiced — for security teams. This time around, perhaps in acknowledgement of how little cybersecurity advice is actually heeded around edge devices, Mandiant and GTIG researchers offered organizations three potential options for how to protect themselves, based on their operational needs, risk tolerance, and whether they've already found evidence of compromise. First and foremost, researchers advised that customers patch. They also suggested isolating at-risk appliances — terminating access paths, restricting outbound traffic to vendor endpoints only, and redeploying from clean images. Organizations can also apply compensating controls of various kinds: network restrictions, such as placing a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in front of edge appliances; credential and configuration hygiene, rotating credentials, reviewing and revoking sessions, etc.; and control plane restrictions, minimizing permissions, keeping credentials in an external vault rather than the appliance's built-in vault; along with plenty more. A Bad Week for Network Security Vendors Edge device bugs are like the milkman: they come pretty reliably every week (and you're going to have problems if you miss them). Even still, the past few days have producede several serious ones. It all began on Oct. 13, when researchers from Volexity revealed that an unknown threat actor has been abusing a zero-day exploit chain in fully updated Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliances. The chain combined all of the worst kinds of vulnerabilities out there: authentication bypass, remote code execution (RCE), and privilege escalation. The former two, tracked together as CVE-2026-104935, earned a "high" CVSS score of 8.6 out of 10. The next day brought CVE-2026-76519, a vulnerability in the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of Cisco's Secure Email Gateway (SEG), which allowed remote attackers to write arbitrary files to the device's operating system. That issue earned a cool CVSS 9.8 out of 10, and was added to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog the same day. Also added to CISA's KEV catalog that same day was CVE-2026-0322, a high-severity RCE vulnerability with an 8.6 CVSS score in Palo Alto Networks's PAN-OS, the operating system underpinning all of the vendor's Firewall technology. A day later, Mandiant and GTIG released its Armory Castle research. Separately, GreyNoise published a blog post about a threat actor it tracks as "skynox7" building a residential proxy network out of unpatched, Internet-exposed household appliances like network-attached storage (NAS) and network video recorders (NVRs). "At this point, these types of vulnerabilities in network devices or tools that manage large portions of the IT of an organization are happening one every month or so," laments Bambenek Consulting president John Bambenek. "Enterprises need to stand up in unison and tell these companies it's time to get serious about security."
402aaeff71af9a09: Attackers are exploiting a critical flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that lets a sender with no login write files to the appliance's operating system, Cisco said in an advisory on Wednesday. The attacker sends an email with a crafted attachment through the gateway and, if it succeeds, could then run commands as root. The appliance filters an organization's email for spam, malware, and other threats, and only a gateway with the File Reputation service enabled and a Content Scanner Tools package older than version 25.3.0.5525 is vulnerable. The fix has been shipping since September 14 in AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780, the builds Cisco listed as fixed in a hardening release that day, which the company now says covered this flaw. It also arrives as a Content Scanner Tools update, version 25.3.0.5525 or later, which installs without a software upgrade or a restart. Cisco found the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76519 (CVSS score: 9.8), in its own internal security scanning and became aware of the attacks in October. The advisory does not say how many devices were attacked, who is behind the attacks, or whether the attackers obtained root on any of them. Cisco has contacted customers of its managed Secure Email Cloud service whose devices showed "indicators of possible compromise" and says it is engaged in remediation and recovery. Administrators of those managed gateways may not have the command-line access needed to run the compromise check below, and Cisco has already deployed the fixed scanner there, so they need no action to get the fix. Who Is Exposed Both conditions must hold. The File Reputation service, part of the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature that handles attachments, must be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version must be earlier than 25.3.0.5525. Physical and virtual gateways on vulnerable AsyncOS releases are affected. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not. To check the first condition, open Mail Policies > Incoming Mail Policies > Advanced Malware Protection, or the same path under Outgoing Mail Policies, choose a mail policy, and look at the Enable File Reputation box. To check the second, run contentscannerstatus at the CLI, which shows the version and when it was last updated. How to Fix It The quickest route is the scanner update. Gateways with automatic Content Scanner Tools updates turned on need no action once the update has applied, so confirm with contentscannerstatus that the version is 25.3.0.5525 or later rather than assuming it arrived. Where automatic updates are off, run contentscannerupdate at the CLI, or turn them on under Security Services > Service Updates. The full AsyncOS fix is in these first fixed releases: - 15.5: 15.5.5-014 - 16.0: no fixed build. Migrate to a fixed release. - 16.5: 16.5.0-780 - Content Scanner Tools (all licensed and supported AsyncOS releases): 25.3.0.5525 or later Cisco recommends that any gateway earlier than 16.5 move to 16.5.0-780. A 16.0 gateway on 16.0.4-302, the build that fixed September's SQL injection flaw, is not fixed for this one, and the advisory does not list which releases count as licensed and supported for the scanner update. For a 16.0 gateway that stays on 16.0, the scanner version shown by contentscannerstatus is the only confirmation the advisory offers. There is no workaround. For a virtual appliance that shows signs of compromise, Cisco's guidance is a rebuild with new credentials, and it warns that upgrading a compromised instance destroys the forensic data and logs. How to Check for Compromise Cisco's check for attempted exploitation is one command on the appliance: grep "System Security" system_logs. It returns one of three messages: - System Security: Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Compromise detected. Follow the recovery steps below. - System Security: Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Contact Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC). - System Security: No compromise indicator was found. No compromise detected by this check. Upgrade if the device is on an affected release. Run it on every member of a cluster. A clean result is not proof: an attacker with root could remove or hide evidence, so also check firewall and network logs outside the device for unexpected uploads to external IP addresses or downloads from malicious ones. The advisory does not say what the scan looks for. If a Device Is Compromised For a physical appliance, Cisco asks customers to contact TAC and to enable remote access so its engineers can investigate. For a virtual appliance, its steps are: - Preserve forensic data first. Upgrading a compromised instance destroys its logs and evidence. - Deploy a new virtual machine on a fixed release. - Rebuild the configuration without importing any previous configuration file. - Renew the credentials and cryptographic material on the appliance, then keep monitoring for unusual behavior. Cluster members authenticate to each other with SSH key pairs. A compromised member's private keys could give the attacker a way into the others, so Cisco recommends restoring every member of a cluster that contains at least one compromised appliance. Secure Email Cloud customers it has contacted are asked to renew credentials and cryptographic material where possible. The September Release This is the second Secure Email Gateway flaw Cisco has confirmed under attack in a month. On September 14 it disclosed CVE-2026-76461, a SQL injection flaw in the gateway's email parsing that could let an unauthenticated sender run commands as root through a crafted email. That flaw affects every configuration and was added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. The two flaws sit in different parts of the software and have different log checks, and Cisco has not linked the attacks. The same day, Cisco published a hardening release for the gateway and for Secure Email and Web Manager that grouped internally found bugs into five umbrella CVEs by weakness class: CVE-2026-76440, CVE-2026-76441, CVE-2026-20353, and CVE-2026-76443, each scored 9.8, and CVE-2026-76442 at 7.5. dce2d98112cca9f3: A flaw in Linux's vhost subsystem lets a local user read and write kernel memory at will and become root across nearly a decade of kernel versions. In one virtualization setup, it lets an untrusted virtual machine write to the host's memory and hijack the program that runs the virtual machine. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-74580 and named Vghost. Tencent Zhuque Lab, which found the flaw, released a fix on August 3 and published a full write-up on October 12 with working demos of both attacks. There is no public sign it has been exploited yet. vhost is the part of the Linux kernel that speeds up network and other input/output for virtual machines and containers. A local user reaches it by opening a device node, usually /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. On the host, the flaw gives an unprivileged user a reliable way to read and write any kernel address, bypass KASLR, and escalate to root. The attack is deterministic: it needs no memory grooming and no lucky timing. The second attack is narrower. When a virtual machine's virtio device is placed behind a virtual IOMMU with iommu_platform turned on, and vhost runs in device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can trigger the same bug and make the host kernel write out of bounds into the host's QEMU process. From there, a guest can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and take control of where the host process runs next, or crash it. How it works vhost keeps a small cache of the memory mappings behind each virtual ring and the shared queues it uses to move data. A cache hit is treated as proof that the region was already checked. The cache is cleared when the mapping is updated or invalidated and when the queue is reset, but not when the VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR or VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM commands change the ring's addresses or size while the queue is live. With a device IOTLB attached, those commands accept the new addresses without checking them, leaving that check for later. Once the cache is filled, the subsequent check never runs, and vhost continues translating new addresses using the old mapping. The kernel then copies data to or from that pointer without a bounds check, so a write to the used ring or a read of a descriptor lands outside the mapped region. That gives the attacker kernel read and write. The flaw sat in the code for about nine years because it took two reasonable changes to create it. A 2017 change (Linux 4.11) added the cache and its shortcut. A 2020 change (Linux 5.9) moved address checking out of the command and into a later step, removing the check that would otherwise have caught the stale translation. Who is affected, and what to do The flaw affects Linux kernels from 4.11 up to 7.2-rc4. Tencent reproduced the full local-user-to-root chain on five distribution kernels: Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. On Ubuntu, the device node was limited to the kvm group, so the starting point there was a member of that group rather than any user. On the other four tested images, the node was world-readable at mode 0666, so any local user could reach it. The fix (commit de845981da67) clears the cache whenever the ring is reconfigured. Install a kernel that contains it and reboot. The first fixed upstream stable releases are listed below; vendors may also backport the fix without changing their version number. | Stable branch | First fixed version | |---|---| | 5.10.y | 5.10.265 | | 5.15.y | 5.15.216 | | 6.1.y | 6.1.183 | | 6.6.y | 6.6.152 | | 6.12.y | 6.12.104 | | 6.18.y | 6.18.45 | | 7.1.y | 7.1.9 | | 7.2 | 7.2 | Red Hat, Amazon Linux, and Oracle Linux have shipped fixes. Ubuntu has fixed 22.04 and, as of October 13, still lists its 24.04 and 26.04 kernels as in progress. Until a fixed kernel is in place, restrict access to the vhost device nodes. Remove world access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock, limit the owning group to trusted virtualization services, and treat membership in that group as a privilege while the vulnerable kernel is running. There is no interim workaround for the guest-to-host escape; for that path, the patched kernel is the only remedy. The severity, and the AI finder The flaw is rated high, not critical, and the raters disagree on how high. The kernel.org CVE team scores it 8.8 and marks its scope as changed, because the guest-to-host write reaches memory in the host's QEMU process and crosses the boundary between a guest and its host. Red Hat scores it at 7.3 and marks the scope as unchanged, treating the impact as remaining within the host's own trust boundary; it also rates the integrity impact lower. Amazon scored it 7.8 and Oracle 7.3. The bug was found with help from Corvus AI, a multi-agent system Tencent built for kernel vulnerability research. The upstream fix credits it with an Assisted-by line, and Tencent says the pipeline found the flaw. This is machine-assisted research, not an attack run by AI. It is the same team and pipeline behind an 18-year-old SCTP kernel flaw disclosed in August, which also reached root and, in testing, escaped a container.
6888d3f1bf78a5a7: GitLab has released patches for a maximum-severity security flaw impacting its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) software that could result in arbitrary code execution. "GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," the company said in a Monday advisory. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, has been described as an integer overflow issue. It carries a CVSS score of 10.0. It affects the following versions - - All versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8 - All versions from 19.3 before 19.3.5, and - All versions from 19.4 before 19.4.2 Patches for the flaw are available in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8. Also addressed are three high-severity bugs - - CVE-2026-92883 (CVSS score: 8.7) - A cross-site scripting vulnerability that could allow an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of other users' browser sessions via a specially crafted repository. - CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authorization vulnerability in the downstream pipeline creation service that could allow an authenticated user with Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches. - CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A permissive regular expression vulnerability that could allow a user to poison cached responses for raw repository files, causing targeted users’ CI/CD pipelines to execute specially crafted content and potentially exposing protected environment variables. The disclosure comes weeks after it remediated a critical flaw in AI Gateway (CVE-2026-90970, CVSS score: 9.9) that could have allowed an authenticated user with Duo Agent Platform access to break out of the prompt template sandbox via a specially crafted flow configuration and achieve arbitrary command execution on the AI Gateway. Last month, another maximum-severity security flaw in GitLab CE and EE (CVE-2026-85706, CVSS score: 10.0) witnessed in-the-wild probes within hours of public disclosure.
eef67d66b352919d: Researchers warn that hackers could soon exploit a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-103849) affecting Magento and Adobe Commerce, potentially allowing them to execute arbitrary PHP code on store servers. According to e-commerce security firm Sansec, attacks leveraging the vulnerability, dubbed BlockStrap, have not yet been observed, but threat actors are expected to find a way to exploit it. The researchers based their assessment on identifying four potential attack paths involving CVE-2026-103849 in less than 24 hours. The flaw impacts September versions of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source through 2.4.9 and Adobe Commerce B2B through 1.5.3. The security firm warned that Adobe’s “priority 2” rating of this flaw does not reflect the danger and urgency in this case, despite the more complex attack path. “The attack path is complex, but anyone with an AI agent can reverse-engineer the patch into working exploits in a relatively short time,” stated Sansec states. “That is why we question Adobe's priority 2 rating (patch within 30 days). StyleSmuggler went from a priority 1 hotfix to mass exploitation in three days, and BlockStrap is of similar complexity.” Adobe’s bulletin, published on October 13, describes the flaw as an improper neutralization of special elements used in a template engine, leading to arbitrary code execution. Sansec explains that BlockStrap is a second-pass template engine directive injection that allows attacker-controlled content in a child email template to be signed and processed again at the root level, executing a smuggled {{block}} directive. According to Sansec’s analysis, BlockStrap exposes a gap left by the StyleSmuggler fix in the same email-template engine. Adobe’s fix replaces the generic processing with registered placeholders, preventing exploitation. Sansec says that a plain Composer install isn’t enough to address the risk, and website administrators must apply the 2026-oct release or Adobe’s isolated patch. “BlockStrap and StyleSmuggler are separate fixes. You need both, so keep the September VULN-39341 hotfix in place as well,” Sansec cautions. The e-commerce security company says it will provide an update when it detects mass attack waves, which it expects to occur soon. d0b52638beda04f7: Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-110447, in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud. Multiple administrator reports indicate that attacks began in mid-September, roughly a month before the formal security bulletin, the GitHub advisory, and CVE publication. CVE-2026-110447 impacts richdocumentscode versions before 26.4.303 and resides in the Nextcloud app’s mechanism for starting the bundled Collabora server. The flaw affects only the optional built-in CODE server app. Standalone Collabora Online servers, Docker and RPM/DEB installations, and Nextcloud All-in-One deployments remain unaffected, according to Collabora. The attacks involve sending a malicious request to the app’s proxy.php endpoint, triggering OS command injection. A key prerequisite for successful exploitation is that the built-in CODE server must be stopped (e.g., after a restart, upgrade, crash). Authentication or user interaction is not required. System administrators impacted by malicious activity reported attacks against multiple endpoints dating back to September 10. According to the reports, the attacker planted PHP webshells and used them to search for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. Some users also reported that ransomware operators are exploiting the flaw, but BleepingComputer could not independently confirm this. 788400810f90a806: Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles CVE-2026-104935, a high-severity authentication bypass + RCE vulnerability, was only partially discovered and patched in July, leaving an opening for threat actors to capitalize on. Even when technology vendors discover vulnerabilities before threat actors do, they can still fall victim to zero-day attacks. That's the unfortunate situation Ivanti found itself in this week, as attackers exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) products: a high-severity authentication bypass vulnerability and the follow-on ability for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) in the SSL-VPN and remote-access gateway. The cybersecurity vendor yesterday disclosed both flaws collectively as CVE-2026-104935. "We are aware of exploitation in the wild affecting a limited number of customers at the time of disclosure," Ivanti said in its advisory. But the situation is more complicated than your typical zero-day scenario. According to the advisory, Ivanti actually "discovered a portion of this vulnerability" in July through the vendor's product security program, and patched it with the ICS version 25.1.3.0 release. "We had been working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions when exploitation occurred," Ivanti said. Volexity researchers discovered that a threat actor, tracked as UTA0576, was using a zero-day exploit chain earlier this month that included CVE-2026-104935. The chain compromised ICS appliances that were fully patched at the time. It's unclear what portion of CVE-2026-104935 Ivanti discovered over the summer, but an Ivanti spokesperson confirmed the discovery was made via Ivanti's LLM project, which uses several frontier and open source AI models to find and automatically remediate vulnerabilities in the company's products. But while AI models helped Ivanti get a head start on CVE-2026-104935, it appears threat actors were able to act even quicker. Multiple Zero-Days Exploited Against Ivanti ICS Instances Volexity researchers first detected the malicious activity on Oct. 5 while investigating an incident at "a network security monitoring customer," according to a blog post published Tuesday. A forensic investigation revealed that an ICS appliance was the root cause of the attack that began on Oct. 3, and that UTA0576 used a zero-day exploit chain to compromise the device. "This exploit chain combined an authentication bypass, a remote code execution (RCE), and a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution" Volexity researchers wrote. "The RCE and authentication bypass vulnerabilities are tracked under CVE-2026-104935." The privilege escalation flaw has not been disclosed. Volexity said Ivanti is currently working on a fix for the vulnerability and it will be patched in a future update. UTA0576 actors extracted credentials from the ICS appliance and then engaged in a variety of post-compromise activities, from accessing the organization's Active Directory to deleting exploitation evidence from Ivanti debug logs. Volexity researchers said because the attack was detected and disrupted, it's unclear what UTA0576's ultimate objective was. What is clear, according to Douglas McKee, director of vulnerability intelligence at Rapid7, are the challenges facing vendors today for not just finding vulnerabilities before attackers do, but also fully addressing them before they can be exploited. "Finding the bug is only part of the job," he tells Dark Reading. "Ivanti found a portion of this, fixed it in the newest release back in July, and then had to carry that same fix back across every older supported version still running in the field. That backport window is exactly where this went sideways, because the fix existed but hadn't reached everywhere it needed to be by the time attackers showed up." McKee emphasized that a quiet fix to one version could be a loud signal to attackers. "Attackers pay close attention to what a vendor changes, and an unpatched gap across supported versions is an open invitation to find the same issue somewhere the patch hasn't landed," he says. Vendors are improving at finding their own vulnerabilities, McKee says, which is a positive development. But he stressed that the exploitation clock starts the minute any fix is released. "Closing the distance between 'we have a fix' and 'every customer has the fix' is where a lot of this risk actually lives, and to be fair, is a very hard challenge we have always faced," he says. CVE-2026-104935: Risks & Mitigations The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Tuesday, and gave federal civilian agencies until Oct. 16 to mitigate the flaw, either by updating to a fixed version or disabling appliances. While CVE-2026-104935 received only a high-severity CVSS score of 8.6, McKee says the flaw is extremely serious and should be prioritized by security teams. "What the number can't tell you is that this is already being exploited in the wild as a zero-day, it lives on an Internet-facing VPN appliance, and attackers are chaining it with a second bug," he says. "Those are the things that should be driving how fast organizations move, and together they push the practical risk well above what 8.6 reads like on paper." The threat intelligence company said network and memory forensic investigations are required to identify exploitation activity.

a2dfa0394e0653a8: A suspected advanced threat actor has been observed exploiting a security flaw in Fortinet FortiOS to deliver a previously unreported memory-resident ARM64 malware known as PEERSTITCH. The attack involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS score: 5.4), a path traversal flaw in the command line interpreter of FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager that could allow a privileged attacker to achieve arbitrary write or delete files via specifically crafted arguments to existing commands. It was patched by Fortinet in April 2026. "PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers Daniel Gott and Shawn Westfall said. "Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection." The cybersecurity company said it discovered the activity as part of its prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider that took place in September 2024. The multi-stage network intrusion is being tracked as CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820), with initial access obtained by exploiting a critical Fortinet FortiManager flaw dubbed FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575). Following a successful compromise of the appliance, the attackers are said to have exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material, and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Some of the harvested details are listed below - - The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device - Running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks - Central management SQLite databases - An inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses - Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations - Ciphertext administrative, local, and SSL/VPN credentials - Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates, and private keys The stolen information was then used to conduct network reconnaissance, establish long-term access, intercept network traffic, set up unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls, deploy backdoors, and exploit a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability (i.e., CVE-2025-61624) to deploy PEERSTITCH. The malware is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C. It includes an auto-script designed to download five components from an external server ("23.240.77[.]233:8085") - - pM.js, an environment preparation script (self-deleting) - a.js (saved as index.js), an Emscripten JavaScript runtime module - a.wasm (saved as index.wasm), a compiled WebAssembly binary module - b.js (saved as ipssem.js), a deployment orchestrator script - dd (saved as lldprx), a native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core) The main phase of the attack begins after an execution delay. The orchestrator ("ipssem.js") launches "lldprx," which then serves as a process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons: "/bin/miglogd" and "/bin/iked." Specifically, it locates the running processes associated with the two daemons, enumerates their memory layout, attaches to them using ptrace and halts their execution using PTRACE_INTERRUPT, allocates executable memory and writes malicious code into it, and redirects execution through the injected code. The end goal behind this hooking step is to create a "covert, memory-resident communication bridge" between the two legitimate FortiOS processes instead of using a conventional network connection or file, and use them as a cover to sidestep detection. In particular, the miglogd hook is equipped to recognize a marker in the data passing through the process. This includes two specific markers - - TCP port marker - 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port) - IP address marker - 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching) Once this pattern is identified, it passes the associated session token or identifier to the iked daemon, whose hook later looks for that identifier while handling subsequent VPN sessions. If such a tag exists within that VPN session's injection buffer, it takes an alternative execution path, bypassing default FortiOS security validations. Put differently, the hooks injected into the two FortiOS processes change how the VPN daemon handles particular sessions. Besides deploying PEERSTITCH, the attackers have been observed establishing a separate command-and-control (C2) channel by leveraging the native Apache "mod_md" module on FortiGate firewalls in order to spawn an SSH-based reverse shell. "The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network," the researchers said. "The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols." Although not definitive, it's suspected that the attackers may have exploited other flaws like CVE-2024-26009 and CVE-2024-26008 to carry out this task. However, Unit 42 emphasized that exploiting these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, which none of the affected firewalls held. In addition, CL-STA-0954 has been identified as undertaking various measures to remove forensic artifacts through termination of syslog generation, crash log clearing, logging telemetry disruption, and automatic deletion of rogue administrator accounts and auto-script objects after execution. "This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks," Unit 42 said. "The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware." "By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring." e2089d243155ed7a: A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it. The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape, is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart. It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack. What the Researcher Showed Paulos Yibelo of the security firm pwn.ai found that specially made network packets sent from inside a virtual machine could do three things, he explained in a technical write-up: read the host's memory, crash the host, and run code on it. All three come from the same kernel flaw. Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets. The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it. Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment." "Our research ran through Omega-Pwn, an internal harness combining our own security research tooling with elements of SingularityNET's OmegaClaw architecture. It let us carry hypotheses, code traces, failed attempts, and experimental results across long-running research sessions. GPT-5.6 Sol was the primary reasoning engine. We directed the investigation, challenged its findings, and validated the interesting ones against actual kernel behavior on systems we controlled," Paulos Yibelo told The Hacker News. Vercel said no report in the challenge showed anyone reading a customer's files, secrets, or application data. How Severe It Is, and Who Can Set It Off The kernel's maintainers assigned the flaw CVE-2026-99999 and, in the published record, rated it 9.3 out of 10, or Critical. The U.S. National Vulnerability Database had received that entry but had not yet finished its own review. The same record lists the attack vector as local. In plain terms, the attacker has to already be running code inside a guest, as the researcher was. This is not a flaw that an outsider can exploit by sending packets across the open internet. It is not in CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, and no real-world use has been reported. Why It Reaches Beyond Vercel Vercel Sandbox runs each customer's code in its own Firecracker microVM, a small virtual machine with its own copy of the Linux kernel, on bare-metal Amazon EC2 hosts. That microVM is the wall between one customer and the host, and between one customer and another. The flaw is not in that wall. It is in the Linux kernel's networking code, which the host runs. pwn.ai said Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards, with no misconfiguration it could find. Because almost every large cloud separates customer workloads on the same layer of the Linux kernel, Vercel said that a flaw there poses a risk to shared infrastructure rather than to any one provider. The Fix and the Fixed Versions The fix is a single Linux kernel change, commit 6785011f8b16, written by Red Hat's Michael S. Tsirkin and merged into the mainline kernel. It adds a check that a packet's checksum data cannot point into the IPv4 header before the kernel acts on it, and applies that check at five places in the networking code. The change is deliberately partial. Its author calls it "a defence in depth measure" and notes that a fuller check on the way packets enter the kernel still needs work. The maintainers backported the fix to the stable kernel branches. According to the CVE record, these are the first fixed versions in each supported branch: | Stable branch | First fixed version | |---|---| | 5.10 | 5.10.272 | | 5.15 | 5.15.223 | | 6.1 | 6.1.190 | | 6.6 | 6.6.159 | | 6.12 | 6.12.113 | | 6.18 | 6.18.57 | | 7.2 | 7.2.11 | Linux distributions ship their own kernels and often add this kind of fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's advisory and whether the fix is in the kernel the host is actually running, not only the number from uname. What to Do Update the host kernel to one of the fixed versions above, or to the vendor build that includes the fix, and reboot into it. Updating only a guest's kernel does not fix the host. The sources give no separate workaround for this flaw if you cannot update yet. Where patching has to wait, the usual step is to limit what a break-in could reach. Vercel said it keeps host kernels up to date, disables nested virtualization, and runs each microVM under Firecracker's jailer, which grants the microVM process only the permissions it needs. That does not fix the flaw, but it narrows what an attacker who used it could do. Found in a $1 Million Challenge The flaw was found in a two-week challenge Vercel ran in August that offered up to $1 million in total to anyone who could break out of its sandbox. No single payout reached that figure. The top reward per report was $50,000; Vercel paid $242,000 across 1,285 reports, and this flaw was the one Critical finding. pwn.ai said it found the flaw in three days using its own AI-assisted research system, with the model doing the source-code analysis and human researchers directing the work. 622bd95115275933: ConnectWise has shut down customer access to its Cloud Backup service (formerly SkyKick Cloud Backup) after hackers accessed application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. Reports of the malicious activity began emerging on Friday, with administrators observing unauthorized access to client data in Microsoft 365 tenants due to a potential “SkyKick/CW breach.” Later on the same day, managed cybersecurity and threat detection platform Huntress confirmed the worries, saying that it had identified at least 162 compromised tenants in its environment. For Microsoft 365 backups, the service relies on permissions granted through Microsoft Entra ID. An application identity known as a “service principal” represents the software in a customer’s tenant and enables it to access resources according to the permissions granted. Microsoft 365 tenant breaches In a security advisory, ConnectWise said that it “recently identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment” and shut down application access for its partners and clients. “We have no indicators to date that Cloud Backup partner backup data has been compromised. 9917fb9c5e95cc7a: Microsoft on Tuesday shattered its own Patch Tuesday record by shipping patches for a whopping 1,413 vulnerabilities, including one that it said has come under active exploitation. These include 1,102 flaws in Windows, 134 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 36 in SharePoint Server, and 22 in SQL Server. Of these, more than 670 relate to privilege escalation, followed by over 300 remote code execution flaws and 250 information disclosure flaws. Over 70 flaws are rated Critical in severity. "Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it's the baseline," Dustin Childs, head of Threat Awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), said. "Is AI to blame? Partly. It's accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too." "But AI isn't creating these bugs out of thin air; it's just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it. The volume isn't the real story anymore. What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what's proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month's new normal." The three vulnerabilities of note are listed below - - CVE-2026-96951 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A command injection vulnerability in Windows Shell that allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network. - CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An untrusted search path vulnerability in .NET Framework that allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally. - CVE-2026-92707 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An improperly controlled sequential memory allocation vulnerability in MessagePack-CSharp that allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network. "An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could evade Mark of the Web (MOTW) defenses," the Windows-maker said. "In an email or instant message attack scenario, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file that is designed to exploit the vulnerability." "In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action. For example, an attacker could entice a user to either click a link that directs the user to the attacker's site or send a malicious attachment." It's unclear how the vulnerability is being exploited in real-world attacks, by whom, and who has been targeted. "An authenticated attacker could place a specially crafted .NET assembly on an affected system and register it for loading by a protected process," Microsoft said. "Successful exploitation could bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and allow the attacker to execute code within the protected process. User interaction is not required." "The vulnerability can be triggered when Windows generates a thumbnail or preview; the user does not need to open the file." The development comes amid continued use of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches to discover and remediate security vulnerabilities. "The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower," Adam Barnett, Lead Software Engineer at Rapid7, said. Customers should continue to review each CVE for active exploitation, severity, attack vector, user interaction, and product-specific guidance."

The --http1.1 option asks the tool for HTTP/1.1, and applications set CURLOPT_HTTP_VERSION to CURL_HTTP_VERSION_1_1. curl's documentation calls that setting a request, because an existing connection on another version may be reused. HTTP/2 support in libcurl is a build option. A build without it cannot negotiate HTTP/2, so it cannot reach the upload path the advisory describes. How a Hostile Server Turns the Bug Into Code Execution Daniel Stenberg, curl's lead developer, explained the bug in a post published with the release, and the public report lays out the code path. HTTP/2 carries several transfers over one connection, and libcurl tracks each transfer with an object it calls an easy handle. During an upload, the server stalls the transfer by setting the HTTP/2 window to zero, returning part of the response, and then resetting the stream while keeping the connection open. curl treats the reset as a reason to retry. In cleanup, curl first tells the HTTP/2 layer that the transfer is finished, then flushes the rest of the unsent upload into the same connection. With no transfer registered, those leftover bytes are read as a new request. The line pattern the reporter includes in the uploaded file makes them look like request lines. When they do, a new stream is opened that stores a pointer to the easy handle. The retry completes on a new HTTP/1.1 connection, and the application frees the handle. The old connection still holds the pointer and uses it when the server sends a frame on that stream, which can happen as the program exits. In the reporter's exploit, data the server sends lands in the memory the freed handle had used. A request that goes out leaks local addresses, which the server needs to defeat address space layout randomization (ASLR). A function pointer in that memory is overwritten with bytes from the server, and curl then calls it. Code execution needs the attacker to know the target's exact curl version, architecture, libc allocator and heap layout, to keep two parallel transfers on the right timing, and to fit the payload into about 23 bytes, according to curl's advisory. "The most likely outcome of an attempted attack is rather just a crash," Stenberg wrote, putting the chance of success as slim. The National Vulnerability Database had not analyzed the record as of October 14. The fix is a six-line reorder in lib/multi.c by Stefan Eissing. The HTTP/2 layer now gives up its references to the handle after the leftover upload data has been flushed, not before. These flaws require minimal user interaction; a victim could simply view a malicious file in the Reading Pane or file explorer preview, eliminating the traditional click-to-compromise barrier that many enterprises rely on as a user training backstop. The attack surface is substantial; any user who receives a weaponized document via download can trigger code execution simply by selecting the file. DHCP servers in particular are deployed on internal networks by design and trust inbound traffic from any client requesting an address. CVE-2026-100219 and CVE-2026-105016 in Microsoft QUIC represent exposure on any service using QUIC transport, which is increasingly common in modern web infrastructure. Outlook's position as the default mail client in most enterprise environments and its deep integration with Exchange and Microsoft 365 services means weaponized messages can reach nearly every employee. ebaf37949a88c936: A local privilege escalation exploit published today gains root on OpenBSD 7.9 by chaining a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow with a separate kernel flaw, bypassing OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization and its SMAP and SMEP hardware protections. Security firm Calif, which found and reported the flaws, published a detailed writeup and full proof-of-concept code after OpenBSD shipped patches for both issues in September. The integer overflow in the shmat(4) attach function was fixed in errata 018, shipped September 14 as a reliability fix. The reference-counting use-after-free that completes the chain was fixed separately in errata 026, shipped September 30 as a security fix. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures. OpenBSD 7.8 also received the integer-overflow fix. The integer overflow, the entry point for the full chain, is classified as a reliability fix, not a security fix. No CVE has been assigned for either flaw as of publication. There is no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been used in attacks. The shared-memory attachment counter shm_nattch is defined as a signed 16-bit short with a maximum value of 32,767 in original BSD sources dating to 1988. OpenBSD inherited the type and never widened it. The exploit maps 127 shared-memory segments and forks 259 processes, pushing the counter past its maximum and wrapping it to −32,643. A race condition then triggers a use-after-free: the corrupted reference count causes the kernel to free memory that other processes still use. A separate out-of-bounds write overwrites multicast-membership counters in the kernel. When the affected socket closes, the resulting decrements modify page-table entries, switching a user-memory mapping to supervisor-accessible and bypassing SMAP and SMEP. The exploit then overwrites a function pointer at a predictable kernel address to run its own code. "While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic," researcher Andrew Griffiths wrote. Both the boot-time and best-fit allocators lack base-address randomization, so early-boot structures, including function pointers in the lo0 and enc0 network-interface handlers, land at the same addresses across reboots on the same hardware. The exploit needs no information-disclosure vulnerability. Beyond the two errata, Calif proposes four categories of hardening: safe-unlinking for kernel linked lists (already used by FreeBSD and NetBSD), randomization of the page-table self-referential mapping, kernel-allocator randomization, and compiler-based bounds checking. Calif said it reported the flaws to OpenBSD "earlier this year." The proof-of-concept exploit code is available on GitHub.
871699ef85217136: The credential-theft campaign known as GhostAction has ramped up, targeting more than 30,000 repositories across 3,000 users and organizations. The spike, according to GitGuardian, was observed on October 8 and 9, 2026. "This resulted from compromising the GitHub accounts of about 1,900 users. It attempted to extract 3,174 secrets from public repositories' CI," security researchers Gaetan Ferry and Guillaume Valadon said. GhostAction is the moniker for a supply chain attack campaign targeting developer infrastructure on GitHub. Originally discovered in September 2025, it involves threat actors compromising legitimate developer accounts to inject malicious GitHub Actions automation workflows into software repositories. Attackers have been found to gain write access to repositories using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) or credentials harvested from infostealer logs and dumps. Using the hijacked maintainer account, they push a malicious workflow file disguised under deceptive names such as Security Audit ("security-audit.yml") or GitHub Actions Security ("github_actions_security.yml"). The end goal of the activity is the large-scale theft of continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) secrets, cloud credentials, package registry tokens (like npm, PyPI, and DockerHub), and artificial intelligence (AI) provider API keys. A new wave of GhostAction has been observed since August 31, 2026, with the malicious workflow pushed to hundreds of repositories. "This new wave seems more experimental and manual than previous ones, with the payload evolving over time," GitGuardian said. "Compared with the original GhostAction payload, the first version of this new payload added a git history secret-scanning feature." As previously outlined by Socket and StepSecurity, the history-scanning functionality features secret-detection regular expressions covering AWS key IDs, GitHub and GitLab tokens, AI-related secrets, and cloud API keys. A second version of the payload also captures about two lines of context around every AWS key ID hit so as to pair them with their matching secret access keys. A third and final variant of the payload includes support for retrieving the secret context during the git history scan. "This payload was deployed in multiple phases," GitGuardian said. "First to 160 previously observed victims, then, 20 minutes later, to 28,000 new repositories between October 8 and 9. New waves have been observed, using the same payload, on October 10 and 12. However, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running starting October 9. Those two subsequent waves therefore could not extract any secrets." Interestingly, a subset of the victims from this new burst were previously compromised in the September 2025 and August 2026 waves, indicating the threat actors are banking on unrotated secrets to pull them off.
f459c5923c1f2f1f: A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it. The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it. The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account. Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4. The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install. Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner. Each personal access token acts as the account that owns it, at a permission level chosen when the token is created. While the flaw was open, conversion changed the owner recorded for each token and left its secret unchanged. An attacker could abuse this by creating a token on an account they controlled, converting that account into an organization, and naming another user as its owner. The token would then work at the registry as that user. The named owner was not asked to confirm the change and was not notified, according to Docker and the researchers who reported the flaw. Docker's conversion page has included the sentence "The new owner receives a notification email" since at least August 2024. Within the token's permission level, a transferred token could pull, push, or delete images in the named owner's repositories and in organizations the owner could access. Docker rated the flaw critical because that access "includes publishing images under a legitimate name," it said. In March and April, attackers used stolen publisher credentials to push malicious Trivy images and malicious KICS images to the publishers' own Docker Hub repositories, according to Docker. Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com found the flaw and reported it to Docker, which says it deployed the fix less than four hours after receiving their report. They named the flaw GhostPat. In their technical write-up, the two say they reproduced the flaw twice on consenting test accounts. They logged in to the registry as the target account, created and pushed to a repository in its namespace, pushed to an organization it belonged to, and pulled its private repositories. What Docker's Review Covered Docker reviewed every account conversion made while the flaw was open and compared them with registry logs and token records. It looked for any token used under more than one identity and examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all. "We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited," the company said. Every one of those pushes went to a repository belonging to the converted organization or to its named owner, according to Docker. In the large majority of cases, both accounts belonged to the same person or team. Where it could not confirm that one person controlled both accounts, Docker analyzed the highest-risk public images without running them and found no malware or tampering. Docker's registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used left no record in the logs. For that reason, Docker treated every token transferred by a conversion while the flaw was open as possibly affected, whether or not it had been used. The advisory reports results for pushes. It does not say what Docker found for pulls or deletions made with transferred tokens, including pulls from private repositories. Who Was Notified and What to Check On October 2, Docker emailed the users whose accounts had received transferred tokens and, separately, the owners of the organizations involved. Each email listed the tokens by description and creation date. The advisory does not say how many users or tokens that covers, calling the group only a "limited number" of users. Anyone who did not receive the email was not exposed and has nothing to do, according to Docker. On October 8, Docker deactivated the transferred tokens it had identified. Tokens that their owners had asked to keep were not deactivated. Todd Matens, who publishes a Docker Compose linter called compose-lint, wrote in a blog post that he received two emails on October 2. One was sent to him as an organization owner and the other to his user account. He rotated his two CI tokens and checked the signatures on his 42 published images, tracing each to the CI run that built it. Docker advises users to review their tokens, revoke any they do not recognize or no longer use, and use organization access tokens, not one person's PAT, for automation that belongs to an organization. These details help with those checks: - Open Account settings, then Personal access tokens. The list shows when each token was created and when it was last used. - The researchers describe two traces. One is a token you did not create, whatever its name, because whoever creates a token chooses its description. The other is an organization in the account switcher that you do not remember joining. - Organization access tokens require a Docker Team or Docker Business subscription. They are managed by an organization owner, a company owner, or a custom role with that permission,
3d29c827bc05744d: GitHub has taken the step of expiring unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations 48 hours after creation after researchers found that it was possible for an attacker to push new versions of a different user's package without having to steal their credentials. "Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. "Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window -- ordinary edits don't restart the deadline." The change contains the risk associated with trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership, GitHub said, adding npm also rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events going forward, along with the existing pull_request_target restriction. In an update to its documentation, GitHub states that a newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days, which validates the configuration and binds it to the "repository's immutable identity." The development comes in response to findings from Bloom Security, which discovered a loophole within npm's trusted publishing to take over thousands of packages and trigger a Shai-Hulud-style cascading supply chain attack. The findings were reported to GitHub on June 6, 2026. "Imagine this: an attacker compromises a single package. An AI agent on a popular package maintainer's device autonomously pulls it for a project," security researcher Golan Myers said. "That single endpoint is used to push malicious code to the popular package. All the package users are exposed. All because one person with the correct access was exposed." Trusted publishing was introduced in npm in July 2025 as a credential-free authentication method that allows developers to push npm packages from a CI/CD platform, such as GitHub Actions, using OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens. When trusted publishing is configured, the developer's CI/CD provider generates a short-lived cryptographic token for a specific workflow run that the npm registry verifies against a pre-authorized configuration. This eliminates the need to store, rotate, or manually manage long-lived npm secrets, reducing the risk of credential leaks. It also automatically generates provenance attestations for npm packages, allowing users to establish where a package was built and who published it, thereby strengthening software supply chain security. However, as Bloom Security found, this security architecture suffered from a problem in how it identified that repository, also called a slug (i.e, the combination of the owner or organization and the repository name that's formatted as "owner/repository"). "It records the repository's address, [...] instead of the permanent ID GitHub assigns it, at least until a version is first published from that repository," Myers explained. "It is like a lock that checks the address on the door rather than who owns the house: when the owner moves out, whoever moves in gets the key." Put differently, the numeric IDs that survive through repository renaming and transfers are carried by GitHub's OIDC tokens, but are completely ignored by npm until the first successful publish from that repository. This means the trust is anchored to a name as opposed to an immutable repository ID, a loophole that can be abused by claiming abandoned slugs to inherit their trust. For this attack to succeed, the only prerequisite is that the victim's trusted publisher points to a GitHub slug an attacker can claim, and the repository has never been used to publish a version of the package to npm.
